lesson.opening: How can one ruler govern peoples separated by distance, language, and custom?

sections.heading: The institutional thread
sections.body:
Conquest versus administration

Tribute, provincial rule, and communication

Religious and literary traditions as historical sources

sections.heading: A model to test
sections.body: An empire requires extraction, delegation, and communication as well as force. A chronology of changing rulers should remain attached to cities and institutions that continue across conquests.

sections.heading: Keep the question
sections.body: How can one ruler govern peoples separated by distance, language, and custom?

activities.prompt: Which happened first: “Fall of Nineveh” or “Cyrus takes Babylon”?
activities.hint: Compare the dates on the unit timeline.

activities.prompt: “Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE.” — is that an event claim or an interpretation?
activities.hint: This is an event claim. Claims about why his rule succeeded require additional argument and evidence.

activities.prompt: Put these events back in chronological order.
Put Assyria, Neo-Babylonia, and Achaemenid Persia in sequence without treating them as interchangeable names.
activities.instructions: A few sentences are enough. Cite a passage when it helps.
